claim: Chinese firms' value-added contribution to an iPhone rose from $6.50 (assembly-only, iPhone 3G, 2009) to $104 out of a $409.25 BOM (25.4%, iPhone X, 2017), reflecting expansion beyond assembly into component supply, but China still captures only 10.4% of the iPhone X's $1,000 retail value.
stance_target: China's role in Apple's value chain has moved beyond pure assembly toward genuine (if still minority) component value-added
scope_conditions: iPhone 3G (2009) vs iPhone X (2017) teardown-based value-added analysis
quoted_support: The bill of materials of the iPhone X is estimated at $409.25, of which the Chinese firms jointly contribute $104, about 25.4%. Chinese value-added in the iPhone X is dramatically higher than the $6.5 captured in the iPhone 3G... the Chinese firms together gain 10.4% of the total value added of every iPhone X sold on the global market.
numbers: $104 / $409.25 = 25.4% (iPhone X China value-add share of BOM)

claim: Using value-added rather than gross export value, the US-China bilateral trade deficit attributable to a single iPhone X is $104, not the $332.75 implied by gross export accounting, because gross accounting misattributes Korean, Japanese and other countries' component value (over 45% of the BOM) entirely to China.
stance_target: Gross bilateral trade statistics accurately represent the true US-China trade imbalance attributable to iPhone imports
quoted_support: In terms of value-added, the US deficit with China for the import of one iPhone X is only $104, less than one-third of the figure based on gross value... For every iPhone X imported by the US, current trade statistics mistakenly add $228.75 to its trade deficit with China... gross-value trade statistics overstated the US-China iPhone-related deficit by an estimated $9.65 billion in 2018, about 2.3% of the total bilateral deficit.

claim: Because so much of the iPhone's value-added is non-Chinese, yuan depreciation cannot meaningfully offset US tariffs on iPhones -- a 25% tariff on the iPhone X would require an 'unthinkable' 400% yuan depreciation to fully offset, versus 43.4% for the average Chinese export bundle with lower foreign value-added share.
stance_target: Currency-based tariff mitigation is structurally ineffective for high-foreign-value-added products like the iPhone
scope_conditions: US-China tariff and exchange-rate scenario analysis, 2018-2019
quoted_support: an unthinkable 400% depreciation of the yuan is necessary to eliminate the negative impact of the same tariff levied on the iPhone X... a 43.4% depreciation of the yuan is required to completely cancel the negative impact of a 25% punitive tariff on all Chinese exports to the US.
numbers: 43.4% required yuan depreciation (average Chinese export, 25% tariff)
33.9% average foreign value-added share of Chinese exports

claim: By mid-2019, Apple had already asked major suppliers to evaluate shifting 15-30% of production capacity from China to Southeast Asia, showing diversification planning began years before the 2025 tariff escalation.
stance_target: Timeline for how long Apple's manufacturing diversification has actually been in planning versus execution
scope_conditions: Reported June 2019, citing Nikkei Asian Review
quoted_support: Apple has asked its major suppliers to evaluate the cost implications of shifting 15-30% of their production capacity from China to Southeast Asia (Li and Cheng 2019).
